title: Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles

epigraph.quote: We believe all the key portfolio decisions that were to be taken for this stage of our business plan have been addressed and we can focus then on execution.
epigraph.author: Parag Satpute, MD & Group CEO, Greaves Cotton Q2 FY27 earnings call, 29 October 2026

web_blocks.text: Greaves Cotton dates itself to 1859. Its own “Built on Legacy” timeline starts with James Greaves, later joined by George Cotton, and runs through a 1939 joint venture with Ruston & Hornsby of the UK to make diesel engines in India [1][4]. The corporate identity on every filing, however, comes from incorporation in 1922 [1]. The working assets are engine design skill, plants around Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (CSN, formerly Aurangabad) and a spares and service network. This chapter shows how they were assembled, what was bought and sold, and why group operating profit swung from ₹272 crore in FY19 to ₹25 crore in FY22 [60].

Control passed in 1947 to industrialist Lala Karam Chand Thapar [1]. Today the promoter is DBH Investment Capital India Private Limited (formerly Karun Carpets), with 55.78% at 31 March 2026 and no pledge of shares; Karan Thapar is Chairman [35][6]. The engine skill came in layers: a 1976 partnership with Lombardini Motori for a light diesel engine unit at CSN, a 1998 partnership with the Piaggio Group, BS-II compliant engines in 2005 and an R&D centre in 2006 [1][4]. BS stands for Bharat Stage, India's tailpipe emission standard, and every step up forces a redesign. Greaves calls itself the largest maker of single-cylinder diesel engines [44].

web_blocks.takeaway: The timeline has two halves. Until about 2006 the company built engine capability slowly with two long-lived partners. Since 2018 it has made a fast run of deals and exits around that engine base, covering electric vehicles, vehicle finance and engineered components. The second half carries most of the risk and most of the explanation for the earnings record below [1][4].

web_blocks.text: The deals since 2018 share one logic: a stable engine maker buying growth outside the engine. Ampere Vehicles came first. The FY19 annual report records a 67% stake for ₹77 crore with an option on another 13% for ₹75.5 crore, and the FY20 report says Greaves completed 100% [13][12]. Ampere became Greaves Electric Mobility Limited (GEML) [41]. In July 2020 it took 74% of Bestway Agencies, an e-rickshaw maker [11]. GEML also holds MLR Auto, which builds L5 three-wheelers (the official class for full-size auto-rickshaws and small cargo carriers) at Toopran in Telangana, taken to 51% in FY24 and 67.41% in June 2025 for ₹55 crore [8][9][6]. In the other direction, Greaves quit construction-equipment manufacturing in mid-FY15 “due to non-viability of operations on account of its continuing losses” [17].

Excel Controlinkage was the one deal aimed at the core. Excel, based in Nagpur, makes push-pull cables and gear-shift levers. Its FY22 turnover was ₹166.5 crore with profit before tax of ₹36.7 crore, and about 40% of revenue was exported [38]. Greaves took 60% on 8 May 2023, 80% on 12 August 2025 and the last 20% for ₹113.47 crore on 13 August 2026 [8][6][2]. Excel's revenue slipped from ₹267.68 crore to ₹252.06 crore in FY26, then grew 14% in Q1 FY27 and 30% in Q2 FY27 [6][25][24].

Management says the portfolio is now tidy. In FY26 it exited finished farm equipment, hurt by Chinese imports, and pruned parts of retail [24][26]. Q2 FY27 still carried ₹60.1 crore of one-offs: an impairment of Bestway goodwill (₹17.6 crore) and the ELE brand (₹2.49 crore), and a faster write-down (₹27.30 crore) of a discontinued “Teja” three-wheeler brand and old two-wheeler tooling [1][2]. The CFO said there was “nothing more at this stage”, yet called such reviews a regular period-end exercise [62].

Some online claims did not survive checking, so we do not use them. Ranipet is described as a closed engine plant, but every annual report shows it as GEML's electric-vehicle plant [59][11][6]. “Anglian Omega” and “Bharat Bharati” appear in no filing or call from FY15 onward [6][17]. Greaves Retail is a division of the parent, not a company [6][52].

Leadership has run in three eras. Sunil Pahilajani was MD and CEO until 16 September 2016. Nagesh Basavanhalli was MD and CEO from 27 September 2016, was styled Executive Vice Chairman by 2022-23, became Non-Executive Vice Chairman on 12 May 2023 and stepped down on 30 April 2025 [15][12][9][6][7]. Dr Arup Basu, who became Deputy MD in May 2022, was MD from 12 August 2022 until he resigned on 14 April 2025, so the two overlapped as executive leaders during 2022-23 [9][6]. Parag Satpute has been MD & Group CEO since 14 April 2025 on a five-year term [6]. The CFO also changed (Manish Poddar replaced Akhila Balachandar, who resigned on 19 March 2026), as did the auditor (Price Waterhouse replaced Deloitte from FY26) [26][6][7]. FY26 is the new team's first full year, so its record is short.

Greaves.Next is that team's plan, unveiled on 6 November 2025 [28]. Its three moves are Accelerate the Core, Build New Muscle onto the Core, and Expand into New Horizons, applied to Energy, Mobility and Industrial Solutions plus two investees, GEML and the EV lender Greaves Finance (GFL) [28][4]. Targets are 16-20% organic revenue growth a year for four to five years, core EBITDA margins of 13-15% and ₹500-700 crore of investment [28][1][4]. EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, a plain measure of operating profit. An older board vision of ₹15,000 crore of group revenue by 2030 sits above the plan [31][30]. From FY26's ₹3,437 crore that needs about 44.5% growth a year (our arithmetic); an analyst said “around 50%” [28]. Core revenue grew 16% in FY26 and 20% in H1 FY27, so the organic target is within reach of the record, but the 2030 figure needs acquisitions far larger than any deal on the timeline [4][1].

The quarter ended 30 September 2023 is the most important single event in the recent record. FAME-II was a central scheme paying a demand incentive on each electric vehicle sold, on condition that makers localised manufacturing under a Phased Manufacturing Programme. On 25 May 2023 the Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) told GEML it had not followed that programme and proposed to recover the ₹124.91 crore of subsidy paid, plus interest, and deregister GEML [8][18]. GEML denied the allegations but, to avoid a prolonged dispute, refunded ₹139.98 crore (subsidy plus ₹15.07 crore interest) on 27 October 2023 and provided in full for a ₹337.34 crore subsidy receivable. Together that is the ₹477.32 crore provision [8][18][19]. A ₹104.20 crore Pune land-sale gain offset part of it, and the quarter's profit after tax was ₹(374.59) crore [19].

The cash cost was the ₹139.98 crore refund; the receivable was income GEML had counted on and will never collect. Without eligibility GEML could not pass on the incentive: prices rose by ₹10,000-20,000 and electric two-wheeler volume fell from 1,08,710 in FY23 to 47,818 in FY24, down 56% [36]. Share recovered from about 3.1% in H1 FY25 to 4.8% in H1 FY27 [1]. Our judgement: this was a subsidy-compliance failure at the subsidiary, not an engine-business failure, since the parent's EBITDA margin was 13% in FY24 [8]. The filings we read do not say whether MHI formally restored full eligibility [33][54].

GEML has needed three equity infusions in four years: about ₹1,170.81 crore from Abdul Latif Jameel (ALJ) in June 2022 [9], ₹29.5 crore from minority holders in FY25 [6], and a ₹530 crore rights issue in July 2026 (Greaves ₹331.12 crore, ALJ's vehicle ₹198.87 crore), leaving holdings near 62.5% and 37.5% [2]. The IPO meant to fund growth was not pursued. GEML filed its draft prospectus on 23 December 2024 for a fresh issue of up to ₹1,000 crore plus sales of shares by Greaves and ALJ [37][36], and SEBI issued observations in May 2025 [6][68]. Karan Thapar explained that ALJ “did not want to be a promoter post a public listing” and so would have to dilute [29]. In February 2026 the then CFO still said “we will be raising approximately a primary of 1,000 crores” [27].

Then the plan changed. The Q2 FY27 results say GEML “decided not to proceed with its proposed IPO and did not avail the one-time extension of SEBI observations”, and ₹12.66 crore of IPO costs became an exceptional charge [2]. On 29 October GEML's MD, Vikas Singh, said the matter is “underway with the IPO committee” and “we are not stating a definite date” [24]. Our read: the 2024 filing has lapsed, any listing needs a fresh one, and an IPO is an option, not a plan. The CFO said the rights money covers the cash burn for 12-18 months [24].

web_blocks.caption: Ten fiscal years of headline results, consolidated (₹ crore), with the parent's own margin alongside
web_blocks.takeaway: Read the two margin columns together. The parent's margin fell from 14% to 4% and was back at 13% by FY24, but the group margin stayed in single digits because the loss-making electric business sits inside the consolidated numbers. Revenue stayed near ₹1,600-2,000 crore from FY15 to FY20, fell to ₹1,500 crore in FY21, then rose 58% in FY23 mainly as Ampere scaled, so group growth since then has come largely from lower-margin investees. Figures are from the aggregator table cross-checked to annual reports [60][11][8][6][2].

web_blocks.text: The earnings cycle has three phases. In FY15-FY19 the engine business ran at 12-17% standalone EBITDA margins and group revenue stayed between ₹1,616 crore and ₹2,015 crore [60][8]. Margin and cash were the story, not growth. Operating cash flow stayed positive every year, from ₹114 crore to ₹280 crore, and the company paid out 59-74% of profit as dividends [60].

The second phase, FY20-FY22, was a squeeze from every side. BS-VI forced redesigns, COVID cut FY21 revenue 21%, and then came what the FY22 report called a “continuous increase in RMC due to exceptional commodity inflation”, where RMC is raw-material cost [12][11][10]. A chip shortage and weaker three-wheeler sales added to it. The parent's margin fell from 13% to 7% to 4%, its revenue from ₹1,988 crore in FY19 to ₹1,178 crore in FY22, and its ROCE (profit on capital employed) from 27% to 4% [8][6]. Group EBITDA margin hit 1.5% in FY22 and group operating cash flow turned negative for the first time in the series, at ₹(56) crore [60].

The third phase, FY23-FY26, is two stories at once. The parent recovered to 13% by FY24 and 14% by FY26, on revenue of ₹2,365 crore, and ROCE reached 21% [8][6]. The core businesses earned ₹383 crore of EBITDA at 14.4% in FY26 [4]. GEML's EBITDA margin improved only from about -30% to about -20% [26][4], so group EBITDA rose from ₹136 crore to ₹239 crore, a 7.0% margin [4]. In H1 FY27 the core margin slipped from 14.9% to 12.0% as commodity prices rose after developments in West Asia and customer price indexation lagged; the group margin was 6.0% [1][25]. Weak operating cash flow, about ₹(334) crore over FY22-FY26, is covered in Chapter 6 [60][2].

web_blocks.mechanism: A legacy petrol two-wheeler maker scaled electric models on its existing dealer network, service reach, procurement scale and captive finance, not on a separate start-up cost base.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: TVS registered 4,72,270 electric two-wheelers in January-October 2026, a 26.28% share and +84.5% on the year, and 60,433 in October (27.0%) [85][84]. TVS, Bajaj and Hero together took 81% of October's incremental volume and lifted their combined share from 53.0% to 62.3% [84]. Ampere registered 82,738 year to date (4.60%) [85]. TVS's own EV-segment profitability was not found.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: In India the “legacy company reinvents itself around electric” story has so far gone to larger two-wheeler incumbents with dense dealers and low-cost capital, not to an engine supplier's subsidiary. Greaves's path rests on dealer throughput (18 to 25 units a month per dealer) and parent funding, not on a transferable moat [1][24].

web_blocks.title: What the history means for an owner
paragraphs: Greaves is two businesses with different histories. The engine and genset core has earned 13-14% margins at parent level for three years and fell back in two squeezes, FY21-FY22 and H1 FY27. So the 13-15% band is a through-the-cycle target, not a floor. We think a return to it is the more likely path once OEM contracts pass on higher costs, which management places from Q4 FY27 [24], but pass-through lags by four to five months, so another dip is possible [62].

The subsidiary has never made an operating profit, lost its subsidy once and has needed new equity three times, with no breakeven date given [24]. Group earnings depend on how fast GEML's loss per unit shrinks, from ₹20,000 to ₹6,300 in a year [1]. The 2030 ambition is a hope; the 16-20% organic target is the figure to test.
The price-cycle record is deliberately held back for Chapter 7, so this chapter has covered business and earnings cycles only.

book_paragraphs: Picture the finance team in early November 2023, closing the books on the September quarter. Sales read ₹727 crore, an ordinary number for a company that had sold engines for the better part of a century. Operating profit read ₹46 crore. Then you scroll to the bottom line and see a net loss of ₹374.59 crore. How does a business founded in 1859 lose that much in three months while its engine plants keep running? You and I will spend this chapter answering that question, because the answer is the key to everything else in this book.

Start with the name. According to the company's own timeline, James Greaves founded the business in 1859 and George Cotton joined later. In 1939 it formed a venture with Ruston & Hornsby of Britain to make diesel engines in India. In 1947 it became an Indian company under industrialist Lala Karam Chand Thapar. In 1976 an Italian partner, Lombardini Motori, helped it set up a light-engine unit near Aurangabad, now called Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. In 1998 it partnered with the Piaggio Group. Notice what the old names give you: not a brand to admire but a set of engine skills that took generations to stack up. Greaves today calls itself the largest maker of single-cylinder diesel engines in India. That is a niche, and niches are where old industrial companies hide their strength.

Peter Lynch's advice was “know what you own, and know why you own it.” For Greaves, that starts with knowing which parts of the company are old and which are new. The engine business is old. Almost everything else in the group was bought, built or sold in the last decade. So when you read about Greaves, keep asking whether the sentence is about the old engine company or the new set of bets around it.

The first big decision was a retreat. In FY15 Greaves quit manufacturing construction equipment, because of “non-viability of operations on account of its continuing losses,” in the words of that year's report. It is not glamorous to say a business is not working, and it is the kind of act you should reward in management. For the next four years the engine business earned 14-17% EBITDA margins at the parent level. EBITDA, if you are new to the term, is operating profit before interest, tax and the accounting charge for wear on equipment. The company paid out most of its profit as dividends, held almost no debt, and revenue barely moved between ₹1,616 crore and ₹2,015 crore. This was a steady, cash-generating engine maker, and a dull one.

Then came the second big decision, and it went the other way. In 2018 Greaves bought 67% of Ampere Vehicles, an electric two-wheeler start-up, for ₹77 crore, and by FY20 it owned all of it. Why would an engine maker do that? Because the diesel three-wheeler engine industry is, in a rating agency's later words, “continuously shrinking amid rising environmental concerns.” A company that makes its living from one engine type has to ask what happens when the engine type fades. The decision was reasonable. The question for you is whether the execution has matched it.

Next came a stretch where nothing worked at once. India moved to the tougher BS-VI emission standard, which forced engine redesigns. COVID hit in FY21 and revenue fell 21%. Then commodity prices surged, and the FY22 annual report records a “continuous increase in RMC due to exceptional commodity inflation,” where RMC means raw-material cost. A chip shortage and weak three-wheeler sales piled on. The parent's margin slid from 13% to 7% to 4%, and its return on capital from 27% to 4%. At group level the margin touched 1.5% in FY22. If you remember one lesson from this period, make it this: engine makers do not choose their input costs, and when metals jump faster than they can raise prices, margins thin quickly.

Money arrived next. In June 2022 Abdul Latif Jameel International invested about ₹1,170.81 crore for 35.80% of the electric arm, now Greaves Electric Mobility Limited, or GEML. In 2023 Greaves began buying Excel Controlinkage, a Nagpur maker of push-pull cables, which are the steel cables inside a sheath that carry a pull or push from a driver's lever to a throttle or gear. Excel was the one acquisition aimed at the core vehicle-components side of the house, and Greaves now owns all of it after paying ₹113.47 crore for the last 20% in August 2026.

Now we come back to that bad quarter. The electric scooters sold by Ampere had been receiving a government incentive called FAME-II, paid per vehicle on the condition that the maker met local manufacturing rules. In May 2023 the Ministry of Heavy Industries alleged GEML had not followed those rules and proposed to claw back the money and throw GEML out of the scheme. GEML denied the charge, but chose to settle. It refunded ₹139.98 crore and provided in full for a ₹337.34 crore subsidy it was still owed, which together made the ₹477.32 crore provision. A land sale in Pune brought in a ₹104.20 crore gain in the same quarter, and even so the quarter ended with a loss of ₹374.59 crore.

Buffett's line is useful here: “Only when the tide goes out do you learn who's been swimming naked.” The subsidy was the tide. Once eligibility went, GEML had to raise prices by ₹10,000-20,000 and volume fell from 1,08,710 scooters in FY23 to 47,818 in FY24, down 56%. Notice what did not happen. The engine business did not collapse; its parent-level margin was 13% that year. The loss belonged to a subsidiary whose early economics leaned on a rule it had to follow, and the group paid for it.

People changed too. Sunil Pahilajani left in September 2016 and Nagesh Basavanhalli took over as chief executive. Dr Arup Basu became Deputy MD in May 2022 and MD that August. In April 2025 both left and Parag Satpute became MD and Group CEO. A new CFO, Manish Poddar, arrived in 2026, and the auditor changed from Deloitte to Price Waterhouse. When this many faces change in one year, you should do two things. Give the new team credit for decisions that look right, such as exiting farm equipment, which the company described as “very competitive” and hurt by Chinese imports. And withhold full credit until they have a longer record.

The new team's plan is Greaves.Next, announced on 6 November 2025. It aims at 16-20% organic revenue growth a year and 13-15% core margins. Above it sits an older board vision of ₹15,000 crore of revenue by 2030. From FY26's ₹3,437 crore, that needs growth of roughly 44.5% a year; an analyst on the call said “around 50%.” Mr Satpute answered that core growth, acquisitions and investee growth together “should take us towards our stated ambition.” Sir John Templeton warned that the four most dangerous words in investing are “this time it's different.” You do not need to reject the vision to notice that the organic target and the 2030 number are very different things, and that the second needs deals far larger than any on this company's record.

The IPO story belongs here too. GEML filed its draft prospectus in December 2024 and SEBI, the market regulator, issued its observations in May 2025. Karan Thapar explained why the structure mattered: ALJ “did not want to be a promoter post a public listing,” so a listing would force it to sell down. In February 2026 the then CFO still said “we will be raising approximately a primary of 1,000 crores.” Yet in July 2026 GEML chose a ₹530 crore rights issue instead, in which existing owners put in more money: ₹331.12 crore from Greaves and ₹198.87 crore from ALJ. The company let the SEBI window lapse and wrote off ₹12.66 crore of IPO costs. Management now says only that the IPO conversation continues with no date. Treat that as an option, not a plan.

Now look at the whole cycle with Howard Marks' words in mind: “We may never know where we're going, but we'd better have a good idea where we are.” Where are we? The parent's margins have returned to 13-14% for three years, and the core businesses earned 14.4% in FY26. Then, in the first half of FY27, higher metal prices cut the core margin to 12.0% before customer contracts could catch up. The group, meanwhile, earns 6-7% because its electric arm still loses money, although the loss on each scooter has fallen from about ₹20,000 to ₹6,300 in a year. Two businesses, two cycles.

Notice that we have talked only about business cycles, not about the share price. That record is held back for Chapter 7 on purpose, so that nothing in the picture of the business gets bent by what the market did. In the next chapter we leave history and open the factory gates: what exactly does Greaves sell, to whom, and what does each customer pay for?

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A company's history is its habit record. Greaves has a long habit of building engines well and a short one of running start-ups. The September 2023 quarter was the bill for the second habit, and the three-year run of steady engine margins is the dividend of the first. Ask of every future announcement which habit it draws on.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Management's statement that the key portfolio decisions have been taken is a promise you can test. If it is true, the next four quarters should bring fewer write-offs, a shrinking loss at GEML and core margins moving back toward 13%. If one-offs keep arriving, the sentence was early.

web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles
question: How did a 160-year-old engine maker end up owning an electric-scooter business, and what did each turn cost?
